clue.text: It shows that letters have been dropped outside one's address

indicators.note: outside asks for the first piece to be wrapped around the second, holding it within

blocks.clueFragment: It shows that letters have been dropped
blocks.note: the punctuation mark that stands in for missing letters, as in can't
one is I, and the 's comes along as S

explanation.surface: Someone muses on a mark showing dropped letters, perhaps a lazy postal address.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes address a noun, a place letters are sent; the definition is the verb, and one's splits as one plus the 's.
explanation.definitionFit: To apostrophise is to address rhetorically, turning aside to speak to someone absent or to an abstraction.

clue.text: Stoical when left out of football team

indicators.note: left out of tells us to drop the letter for left from the word that follows

blocks.note: as in 'as he arrived', meaning when
L is the abbreviation for left
the Glasgow club

explanation.surface: A player stays philosophical about being dropped from the side.
explanation.walkthrough: Celtic is a Scottish football club in Glasgow; take away its L and put AS in front.
explanation.definitionFit: An ascetic person denies themselves comfort and endures hardship without complaint, much as a Stoic philosopher would.

clue.text: Methodical sort of officer

blocks.note: first meaning: neat, well arranged, systematic
second meaning: an ... officer is the one on duty for the day in a regiment

explanation.walkthrough: Read as one phrase it sounds like a methodical type of officer; the two halves are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is an adjective for tidy, systematic behaviour and also qualifies the duty officer in army usage.

clue.text: Month in France could be a third more

indicators.note: could be suggests the words may become something else once their letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters of these words, without the a

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a French month might run a third longer than usual.
explanation.walkthrough: The a is not fodder; only third and more are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Thermidor was the eleventh month of the French Revolutionary calendar, falling in high summer.

clue.text: Veteran soldier's content

indicators.note: content means what is held inside, so the word sits within the letters of another

blocks.note: the letters inside the word, without its first and last

explanation.surface: An old soldier is satisfied with his lot.
explanation.walkthrough: Content looks like the adjective happy, but it is the noun: what the word soldier's contains.
explanation.definitionFit: An oldie is an informal term for an old person or thing, so a veteran in the general sense.

clue.text: An unenlightened thane he turned out to be!

indicators.note: turned out suggests something turned over and rearranged into a new order

blocks.note: the letters of the two words

explanation.surface: A Scottish noble is exposed as a barbarian after all.
explanation.walkthrough: The paper's text reads 'thane be', a scanning error; the page prints 'thane he', and both H's are needed. A thane was a Scottish feudal lord, as in Macbeth.
explanation.definitionFit: A heathen is a person without religious enlightenment, a pagan, so an unenlightened one in the noun sense.

clue.text: Wind can be wild round most of Corsica

indicators.note: wild suggests letters thrown about without order, so they are rearranged
most of means nearly all, so the last letter is cut off

blocks.note: O is round in shape
the island's name less its final letter

explanation.surface: A gale blows fiercely around the Mediterranean island.
explanation.walkthrough: Round reads as a preposition, but it is the letter O added to the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The sirocco is a hot, dusty Mediterranean wind blowing north from the Sahara, and it does reach Corsica.

clue.text: Tempest perhaps put a stop to this mystery ship

blocks.note: Marie Tempest was a famous English actress, so a Tempest may be a Marie
a celeste (voix celeste) is an organ stop

explanation.surface: A storm halted a ghostly vessel's voyage.
explanation.walkthrough: Tempest suggests a storm and stop a halt; really Tempest is the actress Dame Marie Tempest, and the stop is one on an organ.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mary Celeste was found adrift and deserted in 1872, and the crew's fate remains an unsolved sea mystery.

clue.text: Assistant encloses carbon copy — that's laziness

indicators.note: encloses means one piece shuts the other inside it

blocks.note: an aid can be a helper, as in a nurse's aid
the standard abbreviation, still used on emails
i.e., Latin id est, meaning that is

explanation.surface: An office helper idly hides the duplicate memo.
explanation.walkthrough: A(CC)ID then IE. The dash makes that's look like a link to the definition, but it supplies the last two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Accidie is spiritual sloth, the medieval sin of apathy and listlessness, so a literary word for idleness.

clue.text: Indian city in faintly luminous sketch

indicators.note: in places the first item inside the word that follows it

blocks.note: dim means giving only weak light; it is split to hold the city
the city of the Taj Mahal

explanation.surface: A pale drawing of an Indian city glows faintly.
explanation.definitionFit: A diagram is a simple explanatory drawing, which is what a sketch is.

clue.text: Where to find the top brass, presumably

definitions.text: Where to find the top brass, presumably

blocks.clueFragment: Where to find the top brass
blocks.note: surface reading: where the senior officers of the armed forces are found
setter's reading: top-quality brass instruments, played by a group in uniform

explanation.walkthrough: Top brass is slang for the highest-ranking officers; read literally it means the best trumpets and trombones, and a regimental ensemble has those.
explanation.definitionFit: A military band is a regiment's musicians, largely playing brass instruments, so the brass are literally in it.

clue.text: In-between time for one entering during Lent, perhaps

indicators.note: entering means going inside, so this piece goes into the other

blocks.note: in as in 'in the night', meaning during
Lent is the name of a university term at Cambridge, so an example of a term; split to take the one
the Roman numeral

explanation.surface: Someone asks for a stopgap period for a person joining in the middle of the Lenten season.
explanation.walkthrough: Lent looks like the church season but here is an academic term, used at Cambridge and some other universities.
explanation.definitionFit: An interim is a provisional period between two other states of affairs, a meantime.

clue.text: Honourable code followed by a student

blocks.note: an ethic is a code of moral conduct
taken as written
L for learner, as on the plates of a British learner driver

explanation.surface: A person of honour lives by a code, and a pupil copies them.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethical conduct is morally upright and principled, which is what honourable behaviour is.

clue.text: Small farmer in Australia is conceited

blocks.note: first meaning: Australian slang for a farmer on a small holding, short for cockatoo
second meaning: arrogantly sure of oneself

explanation.surface: An Aussie smallholder has a high opinion of himself.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is Australian slang for a small-scale farmer and also the everyday adjective for being cheeky and over-confident.

clue.text: Daughter, repeatedly at home with illness, is munching away

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation in family trees
at home is IN, and repeatedly means take it twice
a painful inflammation of the joints

explanation.surface: A daughter stuck indoors with a sickness keeps on eating.
explanation.walkthrough: Repeatedly looks like it describes the daughter's stays at home; it doubles the IN.
explanation.definitionFit: Dining out means eating a meal at a restaurant, so munching away from home; away here is part of the definition.

clue.text: It carries daily impressions of the latest race

blocks.note: the latest thing is the newest
a short fast race

explanation.surface: A paper carries daily reports of yesterday's race result.
explanation.walkthrough: Impressions sounds like opinions; it is meant literally, as ink pressed onto paper each day.
explanation.definitionFit: Newsprint is the cheap paper newspapers are printed on, so it bears each day's printed impressions.

clue.text: Having to endure recurrence of verrucas is the limit

indicators.note: recurrence suggests running back, so the word is read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: to last is to endure
a verruca is a wart, usually on the foot

explanation.surface: Someone fed up with returning foot warts declares they've had enough.
explanation.walkthrough: LAST then WARTS backwards. Recurrence sounds medical, matching verrucas, but it signals the reversal.
explanation.definitionFit: The last straw is the final small burden that becomes unbearable, the point beyond which one can take no more.

clue.text: Clasp is loose on the Spanish knife

indicators.note: something loose has come apart, so its letters can be put back in another order

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
el is Spanish for the

explanation.surface: The catch on a Spanish blade has come undone.
explanation.definitionFit: A scalpel is a small, very sharp surgical knife.

clue.text: Play false, but a commercial success

blocks.note: first meaning: to betray, as a verb
second meaning: an event whose tickets or stock all go, as a noun

explanation.surface: A show that cheats its audience still makes money.
explanation.walkthrough: The enumeration (4,3) fits the verb phrase; the noun is often hyphenated or written as one word.
explanation.definitionFit: To sell out is to betray one's principles or allies, and a sell-out is a show or product that sells every unit.

clue.text: Presumably he is paid by the disc jockey?

definitions.text: Presumably he is paid by the disc jockey?

blocks.clueFragment: he is paid by the disc jockey
blocks.note: surface reading: someone on a radio presenter's payroll
setter's reading: the proverb says he who pays the musician calls the tune, and a DJ chooses the tunes

explanation.walkthrough: The proverb is 'he who pays the piper calls the tune'; turned round, whoever calls the tunes, like a DJ, must be paying a musician.
explanation.definitionFit: A piper is a musician who plays the bagpipes or a pipe, the hired player of the proverb.

clue.text: Fuel for so-called mental distress

explanation.surface: Someone seeks something to stoke their anxiety, as it were.
explanation.definitionFit: Propane is a flammable hydrocarbon gas sold in bottles for heating and cooking.

clue.text: Divine drink coming up in form of a pint

in places one piece inside the other

an alcoholic drink made from apples

explanation.walkthrough: Divine looks like the adjective heavenly; it is the verb meaning to foretell.
explanation.definitionFit: To divine the future is to foresee or forecast it, so the verb is a synonym of foretelling.

clue.text: This light boat will work

blocks.note: shall and will both mark the future
op is short for opus, a musical work

explanation.surface: Someone vouches that a small craft will do the job.
explanation.definitionFit: A shallop is a light open boat with oars or a sail, used in shallow waters.

clue.text: Each year we see the old Englishman receiving money

clue.text: Middle Eastern island an Indian queen inhabits

clue.text: Not the sort of patient care one expects in hospital

definitions.text: Not the sort of patient care one expects in hospital
